story.name: Pay versus passion: a career perplexity for teenagers

content.title: Pay versus passion: a career perplexity for teenagers
content.description: I was a victim of career perplexity in my teenage years. I struggled, I failed, I lost hope and above all - I was unguided by my schoolteachers.
content.author: Mahrukh Jiwa

content.text: In the photo: My first batch of students. I am the teacher wearing red shirt.

I have always been a 'good' student in all my academic life. The evidences that speak up for my 'goodness' are my report cards that show A* in all my grades. The skills and attitudes being the other most notable evidences of my goodness as a student but unfortunately couldn't be quoted, as these were never assessed and documented. Like other distinction holders, I was also very concerned about my career.

To mention here, my beloved mother was a home tutor and community teacher. She was my inspiration and I would always accompany her during teaching times. I enjoyed teaching as it filled up my soul and gave me a sense of accomplishment. There were community institutions where I would submit a special request to take me as a teacher because I was younger than their eligibility criteria for teachers. In my tuition class, I would prefer to teach other colleagues rather than being taught. I soon realized that I am a born teacher and would like to pursue it as my career.

As the years were progressing, I would play an 'odd one out' game to exclude the options in order to select the subject streams offered at secondary and higher secondary levels. I was not considering commerce as my field because it was neither leading to highly paid jobs in market nor it was my passion. Engineering could have been the toughest competitor in the selection only if I was not made to believe that I am not good at technical side without even being exposed to it. I was good at science subjects as my exam report shows and I enjoyed learning it too. My final decision ended up to choosing medical as my field of study. Nobody questioned me, as it was an expected decision from high achievers. In those four years, I knew I wanted to be a teacher but my lips remained sealed unless it was necessary to discuss about it.
Giving my valedictory speech as the Aga Khan University Examination Board high achiever and distinction holder (mathematics) at high achievers' ceremony at my school.

The actual tussle began after passing out from college. I was motivated about being a teacher but the  society, relatives and community members would expect me to get enrolled in a medical university. I was told that anyone could be a teacher and you will never be able to make money. Some of them even offered monetary help so that I reconsider my decision. Others tried to mold me emotionally saying that it's money for this world and your service to save lives will reward you in the other world. I knew that medical was not the field I would like to pursue further. I realized that I am a very sensitive person, so much so that even the semi-conscious frog in the laboratory makes my heart skip a beat and the fear of inserting injections in a living human body would make me burst into tears. Poor me who could think of MBBS and nursing only while referring to medical field!

I was confused because career selection was never discussed in school. Fortunately, I was referred to an expert educationist through a community institution. She was a blessing and helped me to regain faith in my passion. She illuminated the further career path in the field of education. And that's when I entered job market as a teacher, proudly introduce myself saying, "I am a teacher by choice and not by chance!"

Now as a career counselor in the capacity of voluntary services, I witness thousands of students living similar story of career perplexity. I see those confused stressed faces juggling with what decision they should take, what if they can't make good money and the list continues. I believe that it's the high time of embedding career education in the curricula from the middle school level to support students in this critical decision of career selection.
